h1: Chill filtration and caramel colouring in whisky, explained plainly
title: Chill Filtration and Caramel in Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: What chill filtration and caramel colouring do to whisky, why distillers use them, why some skip them and what the label tells you.
teaser: Two of the most argued-about words on a whisky label. What they really mean for flavour, colour and the bottle on your shelf.
standfirst: Chill filtration and added caramel colouring both change how a whisky looks. Whether they change how it tastes is debated. This guide explains both processes plainly, why producers use them and how to read a label that says "non-chill filtered" or "natural colour".
sections:
Whisky contains small amounts of fatty acids, esters and proteins that come from the grain, the yeast and the cask. At bottling strength and room temperature they stay dissolved. When the whisky is chilled, served on ice or diluted with water, some of them come out of solution and form a haze.

The haze is harmless. But a cloudy whisky on a cold shop shelf or in a customer's glass can look like a fault. Producers have long tried to avoid it.

In chill filtration, whisky is cooled, typically to somewhere around 0 °C or below, so that the haze-forming compounds come out of solution. It is then pushed through fine filters that catch them. Once warmed again, the filtered whisky stays bright even when chilled or diluted.

The process makes whisky more stable in appearance. Critics argue that it also removes some compounds that contribute to texture and flavour, making the whisky slightly thinner. Supporters argue the effect is small. Blind tasting results are mixed. The answer probably depends on the whisky and how hard it is filtered.

Strength matters. Whiskies bottled at around 46% ABV or higher hold these compounds in solution more easily, which is why many "non-chill filtered" whiskies are bottled at 46% or above. At 40% haze appears more readily, so most standard-strength whiskies are chill filtered.
What "non-chill filtered" means on a label

A whisky labelled non-chill filtered has usually still been filtered to remove cask debris such as charcoal or wood fragments. It simply has not been chilled first. These whiskies may turn cloudy when you add water or ice. That is expected.

For many enthusiasts the label signals a less processed whisky. It is a fair signal of intent but not a guarantee of quality on its own.

Spirit fresh from the still is colourless. All the colour in a whisky comes from the cask, unless colouring is added. Casks vary a great deal. Two casks filled on the same day can give quite different colours after the same number of years. Blenders aiming for a consistent product want every batch to look the same.

So many producers add a small amount of plain caramel colouring, known in the EU as E150a, to adjust the colour. It is made by heating sugar. Scotch whisky regulations allow plain caramel for this purpose. It is widely used in blended whiskies around the world, including many in India. In Indian whisky, which is often based on spirit distilled from molasses and blended with some malt whisky, colour and flavour adjustment rules differ from Scotch, so check the national standards.

Some countries require the label to declare added colour. Others do not. That is why the same whisky may say "mit Farbstoff" in Germany and nothing at all elsewhere.

At the small doses used to correct colour, most tasters cannot reliably detect plain caramel. Some experienced tasters report a faint bitterness or a duller nose in heavily coloured whiskies. The bigger concern for many drinkers is honesty: colour suggests age and cask influence, so a deep amber whisky that got its colour from caramel may look older than it is.

Our guide to whisky maturation and casks explains how cask colour develops naturally.

For a large brand, consistency is the product. A drinker should find the same colour, aroma and taste in every bottle, year after year. Chill filtration and colour adjustment are two tools blenders use alongside cask selection and vatting. Our guide to how whisky blenders keep brands consistent covers the rest.

Smaller distilleries and limited releases often skip both, partly for flavour reasons and partly because their drinkers value the look of an untouched whisky. Neither approach is wrong. What matters is that the label tells you what was done. Then taste the whisky rather than the colour.

To test it yourself, pour a small measure of a non-chill filtered whisky, add a few drops of cold water and watch for haze. Then try the same with a standard bottling. It takes a minute and makes the label words real.
faqs: No. Haze in a non-chill filtered whisky after adding water or ice comes from natural compounds and is harmless.
It may remove some compounds linked to texture and flavour. How much it matters is debated and depends on the whisky.
Why do producers add caramel colouring?
To keep colour consistent from batch to batch, because casks give very different colours even at the same age.
How do I know if colour was added?
Some countries require a declaration on the label. Elsewhere, look for producers who state "natural colour" or ask the brand.
